chapter_theme: A single song at Enkan (எண்கண்): the poet asks Murugan to come on the peacock to the sound of drums and anklets, enter his mind and tell him to praise, know and bow to the red feet; the praise names Rama's war with Lanka, Kumbhakarna shaken, and Indra's place restored.

835.reading: The poet asks Murugan, his shoulders smeared with sandal and kumkum and wreathed with kadamba and champak, his anklets and bells ringing, to mount the peacock and come dancing to the drum's syllables, rejoicing and gracious, enter his mind and tell him: 'praise always, understand, and bow to the red feet'. The praise names Rama, whose monkey burned Lanka, who shattered the proud one's body to dust, shook Kumbhakarna and won with arrows, as uncle, Siva who wears the moon, karanthai, thumbai, konrai and the Ganga as father, and Murugan who settled at Enkan after freeing the gods from fear so Indra could regain his place.
835.nuance: The plea asks not for rescue but for an instruction: செம்பதம் பணிந்திர் என்று மொழிவாயே, that Murugan himself tell the poet to praise and bow. The song chimes on nasal clusters (சந்தனம், திமிர்ந்து, அணிந்து), set to the drum's திந்திமி தந்தன.

links.note: 835 asks Murugan to come on the peacock, enter his mind (சிந்தை அங்கு உளம் புகுந்து) and tell him to praise, understand and bow to the red feet. Tirumanthiram 290 says the Lord came unhindered and entered the heart (மறிப்பறியாது வந்து உள்ளம் புகுந்தான்), and the speaker learned a learning that surpasses. Both join the Lord's entry into the mind with instruction; the Tirumanthiram reports the learning, the song asks for the command.
